title: Spring Lecture #18: Spring Boot Profiles & YAML Explained

questions.question: The app is started with `--spring.profiles.active=staging`. Which configuration files from `src/main/resources` does Spring Boot use?
options: Only `application-staging.properties`; the common file is ignored once a profile is active
`application.properties` plus `application-staging.properties`, with staging values overriding common ones
Only `application.properties`, because profile files must be activated with `@Profile`
All profile files (`-dev`, `-prod`, `-staging`), applied in alphabetical order
questions.explanation: Profile files follow the `application-{profile}.properties` pattern and are loaded in addition to the common file: shared values come from `application.properties`, and the active profile's file overrides keys it redefines. The notes stress that Spring Boot does not ignore the common file. Files of inactive profiles are not loaded.

questions.question: `application.yml` contains the nested block below. How do you read the email in Java with `@Value`?
options: `@Value("${app:support:email}")`
`@Value("${support.email}")`, because only the last two levels are used
`@Value("#{app.support.email}")`, a SpEL expression instead of a placeholder
`@Value("${app.support.email}")`, because YAML is flattened into dotted keys
questions.explanation: YAML is just a nested way of writing the same keys: `app:` / `support:` / `email:` becomes `app.support.email` internally, so you still use dot notation. A colon inside `${...}` means "default value follows", so `${app:support:email}` would look up the key `app` instead.

questions.question: Your team builds one JAR and deploys it to dev and prod servers. Someone suggests putting `spring.profiles.active=prod` inside the packaged `application.properties` before each prod build. What does the lecture recommend instead?
options: Keep one JAR and pass the profile from outside, e.g. `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod` or `--spring.profiles.active=prod`
Build two separate JARs, one per environment, with different `application.properties`
Comment and uncomment the prod settings in the common file before each deployment
Hardcode `prod` values in Java constants so they cannot be changed by mistake
questions.explanation: The notes call hardcoding the prod profile inside the JAR a common mistake: the artifact should be reusable, and the environment (command line, environment variable, Docker/Kubernetes config) decides the profile. Commenting and uncommenting settings is the risky approach that profiles replace.

questions.question: The lecture's project is started with `java -jar profileDemo.jar --spring.profiles.active=dev`. Which port does it use and what does `GET /api/demo/greet` return?
options: Port 8080; `LOCAL: Hello, welcome to my application : 200`
Port 9090; startup fails because `app.welcome.code` is missing from the dev file
Port 9090; `DEV: Hello, welcome to my application : 200`
Port 9090; `DEV: Hello, welcome to my application : null`
questions.explanation: With `dev` active, Boot loads the common file plus `application-dev.properties`: the dev file overrides `app.welcome.message` and sets port 9090, while `app.welcome.code=200` still comes from the common file. A key does not need to be repeated in the profile file to be available.

questions.question: The project is started with no active profile (the `spring.profiles.active` line is commented out). What does `POST /api/notification` return?
options: The app fails to start, because no profile is active so no `NotificationService` bean exists
`Here is a dummy notification`, because with no active profile the `default` profile applies
`Here is a notification`, because the prod bean is the fallback
The app fails to start, because both beans are created and the injection is ambiguous
questions.explanation: When no profile is explicitly activated, Spring treats the `default` profile as active. `DummyNotificationServiceImpl` lists `default`, so it is the only `NotificationService` bean and gets injected; the `prod` bean is skipped. That is exactly why the lecture added "default" to the dummy implementation's `@Profile`.

questions.question: In dev you want a `DummyPaymentService` that never charges cards; in prod a `RealPaymentService`. Separately, the payment gateway URL differs between dev and prod. Which tools does the lecture recommend for each need?
options: Profile-specific files for both: put the class name to instantiate in `application-dev.properties`
`@Profile` for both: annotate a constant holding the URL with `@Profile("dev")`
`@Value` with a default for the implementation, and `@Profile` for the URL
`@Profile` on the two service classes (different implementations), and profile-specific files for the URL (different values)
questions.explanation: The notes' rule: profile-specific files change values (ports, URLs, credentials, messages), while `@Profile` changes which beans/classes are created. Choosing between two implementations is a bean decision, so it uses `@Profile`; a URL is just a value, so it belongs in `application-dev`/`application-prod` files.

questions.question: In the lecture's `DemoController`, what does `System.out.println(names)` print when `/api/demo/greet` is called?
options: A four-element list: [Aditya, Rohit, Rohan, Sohan]
A one-element list whose only item is the whole string
Nothing: startup fails because a `List` can only be injected with the SpEL `split(',')` expression
null, because `@Value` cannot inject collections
questions.explanation: Spring Boot's conversion service converts a comma-separated property value into a `List<String>` with four elements, and `List.toString()` prints them with ", " separators. The SpEL `#{'${...}'.split(',')}` form shown in the notes also works, but the lecture's code shows it is not required for this simple case.

questions.question: A tester runs the lecture's project with `--spring.profiles.active=test`. There is no `application-test.properties`, and the two `NotificationService` implementations are annotated `@Profile({"dev", "default", "staging"})` and `@Profile("prod")`. What happens?
options: It starts with the dummy service, because `default` is always active as a fallback
It starts with both services, because unknown profiles disable `@Profile` checks
Startup fails: `NotificationController` needs a `NotificationService`, but no implementation is active for `test`
It starts normally, but `POST /api/notification` returns 404
questions.explanation: `default` applies only when no profile is active; activating `test` replaces it. Neither implementation matches `test`, so no `NotificationService` bean exists and the controller's constructor injection fails during startup. A missing `application-test.properties` is harmless on its own; the missing bean is the problem.
questions.source: code: DummyNotificationServiceImpl.java, NotificationServiceImpl.java, NotificationController.java; notes p40-p42

questions.question: A developer uncomments `spring.profiles.active=dev` in the packaged `application.properties`. Operations then start that JAR with `java -jar profileDemo.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod`. Which profile is active and which port is used?
options: `dev` on port 9090, because the value inside the JAR is read first
`prod` on port 8191, because command-line arguments take precedence over values in configuration files
Both `dev` and `prod`, with dev's port 9090 because `dev` is listed first
Neither; conflicting values make Spring fall back to the `default` profile on port 8080
questions.explanation: `spring.profiles.active` is an ordinary property, and command-line arguments outrank file-based sources, so `prod` wins and `application-prod.properties` sets port 8191. This is why passing the profile from outside works even if a default is baked into the file. Values are overridden, not merged as two active profiles.

questions.question: Ignoring the lecture's advice, a project has both `application.properties` (`server.port=8080`) and `application.yml` (`server:` / `port: 9090`) in `src/main/resources`. Which port is used, and what is the lesson?
options: 9090, because YAML is the newer format and always wins
The app fails to start, because Spring Boot forbids two config formats
8080, because when both formats are in the same location `.properties` takes precedence, which is exactly the hidden confusion the lecture warns about
A random one of the two, depending on file-system order
questions.explanation: Spring Boot loads both, but the docs state that if `.properties` and YAML files exist in the same location, `.properties` takes precedence. The app starts fine, so nothing tells you the YAML value is being ignored, which is why the notes say to stick to one format per project.
